title: Python Concurrency: GIL, Threads, Processes and asyncio
summary: Quick revision notes on what the GIL blocks and how to pick between threading, multiprocessing, concurrent.futures and asyncio for I/O-bound and CPU-bound work, plus what free-threaded Python 3.13+ changes.

chapters.title: The GIL and Concurrency Mental Model
points: The GIL is a mutex in CPython letting only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, even on multi-core machines
The GIL protects interpreter internals (reference counts); it does not make your compound operations atomic, so `count += 1` still needs a Lock
The GIL is released during blocking I/O (sockets, files, sleep) and in many C extensions (NumPy, hashlib), so threads overlap there
Concurrency vs parallelism: threads and asyncio interleave tasks (concurrency); only multiple processes run Python code in parallel on several cores
Decision rule: I/O-bound waiting on network or disk -> threads or asyncio; CPU-bound number crunching -> processes

chapters.title: Threading for I/O-Bound Work
points: Create and run: `t = threading.Thread(target=fn, args=(x,)); t.start(); t.join()`; join blocks until the thread finishes
Threads share memory, so shared mutable state needs `with lock:` using `threading.Lock()` to avoid race conditions
`daemon=True` threads are killed abruptly when the main thread exits; non-daemon threads keep the program alive
`queue.Queue` is the thread-safe way to pass work between producer and consumer threads; use `put()`, `get()` and `task_done()`
CPU-bound code in threads gives no speedup under the GIL and can run slower due to lock contention and switching

chapters.title: Multiprocessing for CPU-Bound Work
points: Each `multiprocessing.Process` has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so CPU-bound work truly runs in parallel across cores
Always guard the entry point with `if __name__ == '__main__':`; on Windows and macOS (spawn start method) child processes re-import the module and would spawn endlessly
`Pool(n).map(fn, items)` splits work across n workers; use `with Pool() as p:` and `chunksize` for many small tasks
Arguments and return values are pickled between processes: lambdas, open files and sockets cannot be passed, and large objects are costly to copy
Processes do not share memory; use `Queue`, `Pipe`, or `shared_memory` for data exchange, and expect higher startup cost than threads

chapters.title: concurrent.futures Executors
points: `ThreadPoolExecutor` for I/O-bound and `ProcessPoolExecutor` for CPU-bound share one identical interface, so switching is a one-word change
`executor.submit(fn, *args)` returns a `Future`; `future.result(timeout=)` blocks and re-raises any exception from the worker
`executor.map(fn, items)` returns results in input order and raises the first exception when you iterate over it
`as_completed(futures)` yields futures in finish order, useful for progress and handling fast results first; `wait()` blocks until all or first complete
Use `with` so the pool shuts down and joins workers; forgetting `.result()` silently swallows exceptions inside futures

chapters.title: asyncio Basics and Free-Threaded Python 3.13+
points: `async def` defines a coroutine; calling it only creates a coroutine object, and it runs only when awaited or scheduled; start with `asyncio.run(main())`
`await` yields control to the event loop at that point; a single thread runs many tasks cooperatively, so one blocking call (`time.sleep`, `requests.get`) freezes everything

`asyncio.create_task(coro())` starts concurrent execution; `await asyncio.gather(a(), b())` runs awaitables together and returns results in order; `asyncio.TaskGroup` (3.11+) adds structured error handling
Use `await asyncio.sleep()`, not `time.sleep()`; push unavoidable blocking calls off the loop with `await asyncio.to_thread(fn)`

Free-threaded build (PEP 703, `python3.13t`) removes the GIL so threads run Python in parallel; it is experimental in 3.13, with some single-thread slowdown, and extensions must be compatible, while you still need locks for shared state

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Choosing and Using Concurrency Tools
points: Picker: network or disk waiting at modest scale -> `ThreadPoolExecutor`; thousands of connections with async libraries -> `asyncio`; CPU-heavy -> `ProcessPoolExecutor` or `Pool`
Core calls: `Thread(target, args).start()/join()`, `Pool.map`, `executor.submit/map`, `as_completed`, `asyncio.run`, `gather`, `to_thread`
Common errors: missing `__main__` guard, unpicklable arguments, blocking call inside `async def`, un-awaited coroutine, unguarded shared counter
Check GIL status on 3.13+ with `sys._is_gil_enabled()`; run with `PYTHON_GIL=0` or `python3.13t` for free-threaded mode
Rule of thumb: measure first; threads for I/O, processes for CPU, asyncio for massive I/O concurrency, and free-threaded builds only after confirming library support
